opus-5.5.text:
So the tricky thing is that a neural network's weights aren't unique the way people tend to assume. Take a hidden layer with, say, a hundred neurons. You can shuffle those neurons in any order, and as long as you also permute the incoming and outgoing weights to match, you get exactly the same function. Same outputs, same loss, same everything. In weight space, though, those are completely different points. For a layer of size n that's n-factorial equivalent configurations, and it multiplies across every layer. So every trained model you look at is just one representative of a huge equivalence class.

That matters a lot for the work we do on learning from populations of models, what we call model zoos and hyper-representations. If you want to train a network that takes other networks' weights as input, to predict accuracy, generalization, or properties of the training data, or to generate new weights, you have to cope with the fact that two functionally identical models can look totally unrelated as raw vectors. A naive encoder will treat them as different, and it ends up spending its capacity learning the symmetry instead of the structure you actually care about.

You can handle it in a few ways, each with trade-offs. You can try to canonicalize, aligning models to a reference by matching neurons. That's related to the work on weight matching and linear mode connectivity, the "git re-basin" line of thinking. But finding the best permutation is a hard combinatorial problem, so you rely on approximations, and it's not obvious which reference to pick. You can build equivariant architectures that respect the symmetry by construction, which is elegant, but they can be complex and harder to scale to large, heterogeneous architectures. What we've found works well in practice is treating permutations as a data augmentation: during self-supervised training on model zoos, we show the encoder permuted versions of the same model and ask it to map them to similar representations. That's a contrastive, invariance-learning approach, and it scales nicely.

And permutations aren't the only symmetry. With ReLUs you also have scaling symmetries: you can multiply incoming weights by a positive constant and divide the outgoing ones by the same constant. Normalization layers add more. So the real equivalence class is even bigger, and the question is how much invariance you want. Sometimes the specific point in weight space carries information, about training dynamics or initialization for example, and you don't want to throw that away.

So the challenge is balance: you want representations that are robust to these symmetries but still sensitive to what actually distinguishes one model from another. Getting that right is what makes weight space such an interesting data modality to study.

r001.rationale: It states that shuffling hidden-layer neurons while permuting their incoming and outgoing weights accordingly leaves the network’s function and outputs unchanged.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the thing that makes this tricky is really quite fundamental to how neural networks are built. If you take a simple multilayer perceptron and you look at one hidden layer, you can permute the neurons in that layer, and as long as you permute the incoming weights and the outgoing weights consistently, the network computes exactly the same function. Nothing changes from the outside. But the weight vector you'd read out, if you flatten it, looks completely different.

And this scales badly. If you have a layer with, say, a thousand neurons, that's a thousand factorial equivalent arrangements for that one layer alone. Multiply that across layers and you have an astronomical number of weight configurations that are all, functionally, the same model. So when we train a population of models, which is what we do a lot in our work on what we call model zoos, two networks trained from different random seeds that end up at essentially the same solution can sit extremely far apart in the raw weight space, simply because their neurons got shuffled differently.

That's a problem when you want to learn on weights. We've been interested in treating the weights themselves as a data modality, so training a model that takes another model's weights as input and predicts things like its test accuracy, or what dataset it was trained on, or even generating new weights. If your downstream model is not aware of the permutation symmetry, it has to learn all these equivalences from data, and it basically never has enough data to do that. You end up with representations that are brittle. You can show a model the same network, permuted, and it gives you a different answer, which is obviously wrong.

So there are two broad ways people deal with it. One is to build the symmetry into the architecture, so you design equivariant or invariant layers that respect the permutation structure by construction. That's elegant, but it gets complicated quickly once you move beyond simple MLPs to things like convolutions, residual connections, attention, normalization layers. Each one has its own symmetry group and they interact. The other approach is to canonicalize or align the weights, so you find a permutation that maps one network onto another, essentially sorting the neurons into a reference order. Git Re-Basin and related work did this. But the alignment problem itself is combinatorial, you're solving an assignment problem per layer, and it's only approximate for anything nontrivial.

And then what I find genuinely interesting, beyond the practical annoyance, is that the permutation symmetry is also connected to the geometry of the loss landscape. The reason linear mode connectivity sometimes works and sometimes doesn't seems closely tied to whether you've resolved these symmetries. So it's not just a nuisance for representation learning on weights, it tells you something about what the solution space actually looks like. We're still, I think, quite far from fully understanding that.

r001.rationale: The response states that permuting neurons in an MLP hidden layer, while consistently permuting its incoming and outgoing weights, leaves the computed function unchanged.

astra-6.text:
The tricky part is that different points in weight space can represent exactly the same function. If I take the neurons in a hidden layer, reorder them, and correspondingly reorder the connections in the next layer, the network’s output doesn’t change. But if you compare the two sets of weights coordinate by coordinate, they can look quite different.

That becomes a problem when we want to compare networks or interpolate between them. You might think, “Let’s just average the weights,” but neuron number five in one network doesn’t necessarily correspond to neuron number five in another. You first have to figure out an alignment, and those permutations are coupled across layers.

So the question is: How do we build a representation of a neural network that captures what it has learned without being sensitive to this arbitrary ordering of neurons? That’s particularly important when the weights themselves become the data you want to learn from.

r001.rationale: It says that reordering hidden-layer neurons and correspondingly reordering the next layer’s connections leaves the network output unchanged.

sol-6.1.text:
The tricky thing is that two neural networks can have very different weights and still implement exactly the same function. If I reorder the neurons in one hidden layer and make the corresponding change to the connections in the next layer, the network’s behavior doesn’t change. But if you flatten those weights into vectors, they can look very far apart.

So when we talk about distance in weight space, or interpolating between two models, we have to ask: Are we looking at a meaningful difference, or just a different ordering of the neurons? If you average two networks without accounting for that, you might mix together neurons that play completely different roles.

And matching them is difficult because the permutations interact across layers. You can’t necessarily solve each layer independently. That’s what makes weight space interesting: we have this enormous parameter space, but many points are equivalent. The challenge is to build methods that respect that equivalence while still capturing meaningful differences between models.

r001.rationale: The response says reordering neurons in a hidden layer, with the corresponding change to the next layer’s connections, leaves the network’s behavior unchanged.
